title: Automation at Workplaces
tagline: Mechanisation against automation, their merits and demerits, and the productivity tools used in banks, retail, offices and airports.

overview.intro: Automation is the use of technology to perform processes with minimal human intervention, and it has moved from factory floors into the service economy where most people now work. This unit distinguishes mechanisation from automation, traces how the two have developed, weighs the merits and demerits honestly, and then looks at where automation actually appears in four workplaces the syllabus names: banks, the retail industry, corporate offices and airports. The examination value lies in being able to give a concrete example for each sector rather than a general claim about computers.

facts.label: Mechanisation vs automation
facts.value: Mechanisation uses machines to assist human effort; automation runs a process with little or no human intervention, often controlling itself.

facts.label: Evolution
facts.value: First industrial mechanisation, then hard automation in mass production, then computer-controlled flexible automation, then intelligent automation of knowledge work.

facts.label: Merits
facts.value: Speed, accuracy, continuity, lower unit cost, safety in hazardous tasks, better records.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Comparison questions and sector-wise applications are the standard questions in this unit.

learningOutcomes: Define mechanisation and automation and distinguish between them.
Describe the evolution of automation in industry.
State the merits and demerits of automation with examples.
Identify productivity tools used in banks, retail, corporate offices and airports.
Judge when automation is and is not appropriate.

learn.title: Meaning, evolution and the mechanisation distinction

blocks.text: Mechanisation means using machines to perform a task with human effort still directing the work. A worker driving a tractor is mechanised; the machine supplies the power but the operator supplies the judgement. Automation goes a step further: the process runs largely on its own, following a programme and often monitoring itself so that it corrects or stops when conditions change. The distinguishing question is not how much technology is present but how much human intervention the process requires to run and to correct itself.

blocks.caption: Mechanisation against automation
rows: Definition
Machines assist human effort
Process runs with minimal human intervention
Control
Human operator controls each step
Programme or control system directs the process
Judgement
Supplied continuously by the operator
Built into rules, sensors or software
Example
A machine operated by a worker
A robot welding without an operator at the cell
Correction of errors
Made by the operator
Made by the system, or flagged for review

blocks.text: The evolution runs in stages. The first industrial age mechanised production with steam and later electric power. Hard automation followed, where dedicated machines performed one operation repeatedly in mass production. Computer-controlled machines then gave flexible automation, where one line could be reprogrammed for different products. The current stage applies the same idea to information work: software now processes transactions, reads documents and schedules work with little supervision.

The case for automation rests on qualities machines have and people do not sustain: speed, consistency, accuracy, endurance and indifference to monotony or hazard. An automated process runs at a constant rate through the night, produces the same result on the ten thousandth repetition as on the first, keeps a complete electronic record, and can operate in conditions that are unsafe for people. These qualities lower the unit cost of a repetitive process and free staff for work that requires judgement and empathy.

blocks.caption: Merits and demerits of automation
rows: Higher speed and output per hour
High initial investment and long payback
Consistent quality with fewer defects
Reduction in direct employment
Continuous operation without fatigue
Dependence on power, software and maintenance
Safer handling of hazardous processes
Loss of skilled craft and human judgement
Complete and immediate records
Security and privacy risks in stored data
Lower unit cost once installed
Rigidity if the system cannot adapt to exceptions

items: Automate the repetitive, the hazardous and the data-heavy; keep judgement with people.
A system that cannot handle exceptions becomes a bottleneck precisely when cases are unusual.
Retraining staff for supervisory and exception-handling work is part of the cost of the decision, not an optional extra.
Falling unit cost must be weighed against the fixed cost and the cost of downtime.

items.text: A bank posting thousands of interest credits overnight without manual entry.
items.note: Speed, consistency and an audit trail are gained; the human role moves to exception review.

items.text: A fully automated warehouse that stops when a barcode is unreadable.
items.note: Rigidity: the exception that a person would resolve instantly halts the system.

learn.title: Productivity tools in banks, retail, offices and airports

blocks.text: In banks, automation appears in automated teller machines, core banking systems that update a single customer record across branches, electronic fund transfer and real-time gross settlement for interbank payments, and in scoring of loan applications. In the retail industry it appears in barcode scanning at the point of sale, electronic shelf labels, inventory systems that reorder automatically, and online ordering with warehouse picking.

blocks.caption: Automation by workplace
rows: Banks
Core banking, automated teller machines, electronic fund transfer, cheque truncation
Transactions completed in seconds with no branch visit
Retail
Barcode scanning, point-of-sale billing, automatic reordering, self-checkout
Faster billing, accurate stock, fewer pricing errors
Corporate offices
Enterprise resource planning, customer relationship management, electronic mail, workflow approvals
Approvals routed automatically, records centralised, less paper
Airports
Check-in kiosks, baggage handling systems, boarding pass scanners, security screening machines
Higher passenger throughput and traceable baggage

blocks.text: In corporate offices, enterprise resource planning integrates finance, purchase, production and human resources onto one system so that a single transaction updates every report. Customer relationship management systems track every interaction with a customer so that service and sales are informed by history. Workflow systems move approvals automatically to the next person and escalate them when they are late, which is where much of the measurable time saving appears.

items.text: A supermarket chain’s system that reorders stock when the point-of-sale scan drops inventory below a set level.
items.note: Automatic reordering removes both stock-outs and the cost of overstocking caused by guesswork.

items.text: A boarding pass scanned at the gate and matched to the passenger manifest.
items.note: The airport gains throughput and an accurate record of who actually travelled.

blocks.text: Automation is a means and not an end, and the decision should follow the character of the task. A process is a good candidate when it is repetitive, follows rules, handles high volumes, needs a consistent audit trail and is unpleasant or unsafe for people. It is a poor candidate when it is rare, ambiguous, emotionally charged or dependent on context that the system does not hold. Customer complaints about a wrong bill, for example, need a person at the point of resolution even though the calculation of the bill should be automated.

items: Volume and repetition: high volume with steady rules repays the fixed investment.
Tolerance for error: where an error is costly, automation with checks is worth the cost.
Exception rate: a high exception rate makes the system a bottleneck rather than a saving.
Data quality: automation of poor data produces poor output faster and with more authority.
People: plan the redeployment and retraining before installation, not afterwards.

blocks.text: The practical discipline is to separate the process into its rule-based part and its judgement-based part, automate the first, and design the second as a review step. That structure keeps the speed of the machine and the wisdom of the person, and it is the position a good answer to this topic should reach.

keyPoints: Mechanisation uses machines to assist human effort; automation runs a process with minimal intervention.
The test for automation is how much human intervention the process needs to run and to correct itself.
Automation evolved from mechanisation through hard and flexible automation to intelligent automation.
Merits: speed, consistency, accuracy, continuous operation, safety and lower unit cost.
Demerits: high initial cost, job losses, dependence on power and software, rigidity and security risk.
Banks automate through core banking, automated teller machines and electronic fund transfer.
Retail automates through barcode billing, point-of-sale systems and automatic reordering.
Corporate offices use enterprise resource planning, customer relationship management and workflow approvals.
Airports automate check-in, baggage handling, boarding scans and security screening.
Automate the repetitive and the hazardous; keep judgement with people.
examFocus: Comparison questions on mechanisation and automation are marked on the control and judgement distinction, not on the amount of machinery.
Application questions want a named tool per sector: give the tool and say what it improves.
Merit and demerit answers earn more when each point is paired with a concrete workplace example.

vocabulary.meaning: Use of technology to perform a process with minimal human intervention.
Use of machines to perform work while a human still directs the process.
Computer-controlled equipment that can be reprogrammed for different products.
System in which every branch updates one shared customer record in real time.
Billing system where the sale, stock and price records are updated at the checkout.
Software that routes approvals to the next person and escalates delays.
Dealing with cases that fall outside the system’s rules, which still needs people.

questions.prompt: The essential difference between mechanisation and automation is:
options: Automation uses electronics while mechanisation uses gears
Automation requires little human intervention to run and correct the process
questions.answer: Automation requires little human intervention to run and correct the process
questions.explanation: The deciding factor is how much human direction and correction the process needs, not what the machine is made of or where it is used.

questions.prompt: Barcode scanning at a supermarket checkout is an example of automation in:
questions.explanation: Point-of-sale barcode billing updates price, stock and sales records in the retail industry at the moment of sale.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a DEMERIT of automation?
options: High initial investment and dependence on power and software
Ability to work in hazardous conditions
Lower unit cost at high volume
questions.answer: High initial investment and dependence on power and software
questions.explanation: The other three are merits; the fixed cost, maintenance and dependence on uninterrupted power and correct software are the costs side of the decision.

questions.prompt: Which task is the WEAKEST candidate for full automation?
options: Crediting interest on savings accounts overnight
Scanning boarding passes at a gate
Resolving an emotionally charged customer complaint about a wrongly billed account
Reordering stock when sales fall below a set level
questions.answer: Resolving an emotionally charged customer complaint about a wrongly billed account
questions.explanation: The complaint is ambiguous, emotionally charged and context-dependent, so a person must handle it even though the calculation behind the bill should be automated.

questions.prompt: The banking system in which every branch updates one shared customer record in real time is called __________ banking.
questions.explanation: Core banking removes the need for a customer to visit her home branch, since the record is common and updated instantly everywhere.

questions.prompt: The stage of automation in which software processes transactions and documents with little supervision is often called intelligent __________ .
questions.explanation: The term marks the extension of automation from physical operations to information work, where judgement is encoded in rules and models.

questions.answer: Four merits are: higher speed and output per hour than manual processing; consistent quality with fewer defects because the process does not tire; continuous operation through the night and through hazardous conditions; and a lower unit cost once the investment has been made. Complete electronic records are also a merit.
questions.explanation: Each merit needs to be tied to what a machine does better than a person, not merely asserted.

questions.prompt: Mention four productivity tools used in corporate offices and state what each improves.
questions.answer: Enterprise resource planning integrates finance, purchase, production and human resources so that one transaction updates every report. Customer relationship management records every customer interaction so that service and sales work from the same history. Electronic mail and messaging cut the time of internal communication. Workflow systems route approvals to the next person automatically and escalate delays, which removes waiting time from the approval cycle.
questions.explanation: Four named tools are required, each with the specific productivity gain it delivers.

questions.prompt: Explain the merits and demerits of automation with examples from any two workplaces.
questions.answer: The merits are speed, as when a bank credits thousands of interest entries overnight in seconds; consistency and accuracy, as when barcode billing removes manual pricing errors in a supermarket; continuity, because automated systems work without fatigue; safety, as in robotic handling of hazardous material; and lower unit cost at volume once installed. The demerits are the high initial investment and long payback period, which can be prohibitive for a small firm; the reduction in direct employment and the need to retrain staff for supervisory work; dependence on uninterrupted power, correct software and maintenance, so a failure stops the whole process; rigidity in the face of exceptions, as when an unreadable barcode halts an automated warehouse; and the security and privacy risks of holding large volumes of data.
questions.explanation: Full marks need at least three merits and three demerits, each with a workplace example, and a closing judgement about what should not be automated.

questions.prompt: A regional bank is considering replacing its counter staff with self-service kiosks for deposits, withdrawals and balance enquiries. Evaluate the proposal on merits, demerits and what should be handled by people.
questions.answer: The merits are clear: faster service with shorter queues, consistent and correctly calculated postings, an electronic audit trail for every transaction, lower transaction cost per customer and longer effective service hours. The demerits are a substantial capital outlay for hardware and software, maintenance and security costs, dependence on power and network availability, and the exclusion of customers who are elderly, disabled or unfamiliar with machines, which risks losing precisely the segment the bank serves. The balanced position is to automate the rule-based transactions such as cash deposit, withdrawal and balance enquiry, and to keep people for exception cases such as mismatched signatures, large or unusual transactions, account opening with its documentation checks, complaints and lending decisions. Staff must be retrained from processing to advising, and the kiosk floor still needs an attendant, because the exception rate, not the average case, decides whether the scheme works.
questions.explanation: The answer is marked on weighing both sides and then drawing the automation boundary explicitly, since a proposal evaluated on benefits alone shows no judgement.
